system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2206-01-03 18:44:00 to 2206-01-04 15:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with primary progressive multiple sclerosis, neurogenic bladder with a chronic suprapubic catheter, and a history of recurrent drug-resistant urinary tract infections, was admitted for confusion and fever. He was found to have sepsis due to Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteremia originating from an obstructing left ureteral stone causing hydronephrosis. He underwent urgent placement of a left percutaneous nephrostomy for drainage and was started on IV antibiotics. Blood cultures cleared, and he transitioned to oral ciprofloxacin. His condition improved with normalized kidney function and resolution of infection. He was discharged home with instructions to complete a 14-day antibiotic course, restart suppressive fosfomycin therapy, follow up with urology for surgical evaluation of stone burden, and schedule pulmonary function testing prior to any procedure.

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  RENAL U.S.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with MS, chronic suprapubic cath, bilateral
nephrostomy tubes for renal calculi, now w/ hematuria from L nephrostomy.

TECHNIQUE:  Grey scale and color Doppler ultrasound images of the kidneys were
obtained.

COMPARISON:  CTU dated ___.
Renal ultrasound dated ___.

FINDINGS: 

The right kidney measures 10.3 cm. The left kidney measures 10.7 cm. There is
no hydronephrosis or masses bilaterally.  Normal cortical echogenicity and
corticomedullary differentiation are seen bilaterally.  Renal stones are
better assessed on CT.

The bladder is collapsed around a Foley catheter.

IMPRESSION:


1. No hydronephrosis bilaterally.
2. Renal stones were better assessed on prior CTU.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with MS and neurogenic bladder, now s/p bilateral
nephrostomy tubes. Patient w/ new onset L nephrostomy bloody output and
hematuria in suprapubic catheter bag.  // Nephrostogram bilateral

COMPARISON:  ___

TECHNIQUE:  OPERATORS: Dr. ___, Interventional Radiology Fellow and Dr.
___, attending radiologist performed the procedure. Dr. ___
personally supervised the trainee during the key components of the procedure
and has reviewed and agrees with the trainee's findings.
ANESTHESIA: Moderate sedation was provided by administrating divided doses of
100mcg of fentanyl and 1 mg of midazolam throughout the total intra-service
time of 20 minutes during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were
continuously monitored by an independent trained radiology nurse. 1% lidocaine
was injected in the skin and subcutaneous tissues overlying the access site.
MEDICATIONS: Fentanyl, Versed.
CONTRAST: 25 ml of Optiray contrast.
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  3.8 min, 10 mGy

PROCEDURE:  1. Bilateral diagnostic antegrade nephrostogram.
2.  Left nephrostomy upsize to 10 ___ nephrostomy tube.
3.  Exchange of 8 ___ right nephrostomy tube.

PROCEDURE DETAILS: Following the discussion of the risks, benefits and
alternatives to the procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the
patient.The patient was then brought to the angiography suite and placed prone
on the exam table. A pre-procedure time-out was performed per ___ protocol. 
The right and left flank was prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion.

Diluted contrast was injected into the left nephrostomy to confirm catheter
position. The image was stored on PACS. Local anesthesia was administered with
instillation of lidocaine jelly and 1% subcutaneous lidocaine injection. The
catheter was cut.  A ___ wire was advanced into the left nephrostomy tube
and advanced into the distal ureter. The stay sutures were cut and the
catheter was removed over the wire. A new 10 ___ nephrostomy catheter was
flushed and advanced with its plastic stiffener over the wire into appropriate
position. The wire and stiffener were removed and the pigtail was formed.
Contrast injection confirmed appropriate positioning. The final image was
saved. The catheter was then flushed, stay sutures applied and the catheter

Successful bilateral nephrostomy tube exchanges, as above.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. I understand your home health aide noticed your nephrostomy bag has darker red fluid than usual. Can you tell me if you're feeling any pain or discomfort?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I don’t feel any pain. But the color change worried my aide. It used to be just a little pink, now it’s darker red.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We also noticed the right nephrostomy tube wasn’t draining well. Given your history with kidney stones and recent infection, we wanted to check things closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just got out of the hospital for that infection. I’m on ciprofloxacin now. Is this related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The urine test still shows blood and signs of infection, but your vitals are stable and you’re not running a fever. We’re not seeing signs of active sepsis this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why the color change? Is something bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The imaging and nephrostogram showed that your left tube was bleeding a bit from the tract. The right one was clogged. We’ve replaced both tubes to make sure they drain properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Both? Was that painful?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were given mild sedation, and the team said you tolerated it very well. The right tube was exchanged, and the left one was upsized to help with the bleeding and improve drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Upsized? Does that mean it’s bigger now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the left tube is now a bit larger to help keep the tract open and reduce irritation. It should help prevent future blockages and bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But my blood levels—are they okay? I remember last time my hemoglobin dropped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your hemoglobin was 10.2 when you came in, which is stable for you. This morning it’s 8.4, but we expect some drop after the procedure. You’re not showing signs of active bleeding, so we’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. It’s expected after tube manipulation. We’ll repeat the blood test in a week to make sure it’s not dropping further. No transfusion needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well overnight. Vitals are stable, and your tubes are draining appropriately. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Should I keep doing anything different at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your ciprofloxacin as prescribed. Watch for fever, pain, or sudden changes in output. Also, please get a CBC blood test early this week and send the results to your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my ulcers? My aide checks them, but they’re still slow to heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please keep up with your wound care. The note mentions your sacral and shin ulcers are stage 2. Make sure your home health team continues regular dressing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll send all instructions to your home health team. Call if output stops or if you feel unwell. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge—your tubes look clean, no swelling or leakage. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll follow up on the blood test and keep an eye on things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Continue all your regular medications, including the omeprazole and mirtazapine. And don’t hesitate to reach out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge paperwork is ready. You’re doing well—just keep monitoring your tube output and stay on the antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Rest well, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___, a man with primary progressive multiple sclerosis and neurogenic bladder, was admitted due to darker red output from his bilateral nephrostomy tubes and absent drainage from the right tube. He had no pain or fever. He was recently discharged after treatment for urosepsis and was continuing oral ciprofloxacin. Imaging and nephrostogram revealed a clogged right tube and bleeding from the left nephrostomy tract. Both tubes were replaced, with the left upsized to improve drainage and reduce bleeding. He was observed overnight, remained stable, and his hemoglobin showed an expected post-procedure drop. He was discharged home with instructions to continue antibiotics, monitor tube output, and complete a CBC in one week. Wound care for existing pressure ulcers was emphasized.
